title: Duke Ellington's touring and Harrison Smith's early contract
summary: Gil marvels at Ellington's travel schedule and his private pullman car. Johnston mentions publisher Harrison Smith.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: The second Monday, yes. He's

with Duke now. And they travel something awful you know. Duke has, you know, the sense of abandonment that comes with age, you know. I realise this, that I have that feeling sometimes that since you know that chronologically it's less than it was, then a little more abandonment comes.

By abandonment I mean laying off a lot of bullshit that you don't want. You know, the things that you don't want to do and so you say the hell with it, you don't want to do this or that. And Duke is in that kind of thing now where they travel all the time. It's really fantastic. I saw them in Berlin in a hotel lobby there. They played Israel two nights before that and before that they played Rumania, Bucharest or somewhere. Then that night they were going to be in Berlin.

Then they were going to be a couple of other places in Europe. Then go to Barcelona and from Barcelona they flew right to Rio in South America and they played a tour of South American. And from there they flew to the Rainbow Grill. And then from the Rainbow Grill they flew to Australia.
So Johnny Cole said he might have to quit
the job because he couldn't take it.
It sounds like Lionel Hampton doesn't it? (LAUGHTER).
Yes, Duke was born in 1899, right? And he's still doing it and everybody's .........
And he's done it all his life.
Yes, he's so used to it.

Well that was one of the things that happened with the black bandleaders. They really had to exist on one night stands. They very rarely got chances to move in to any of these, you know, key clubs or ballrooms or things like that.
I read that one time that, something I didn't know, and that is that Duke's band travelled by pullman car, their own private pullman car when they went out of town.

They would get off at the station of the town they were going to play for a club you know or a special party or something. Or they'd been hired for a dance. They'd go right to the dance or to the job. Work the job and come right back to the pullman car again. They just had their own place. They lived there.
That's right, yes.
That's how he got by in the South. A practical man. He didn't get involved in anything. He knew the situation. He didn't have to kowtow either. Come in there and do it and run right out again, right?
I just had an interview this week with a man who owned Duke's first contract, Harrison Smith.
No kidding, wow!
Yes. And he put out, well he says he's the one who created the word Ellingtonian.
Ellingtonian, yes.
And he also has a flier called Little Farina. You remember Little Farina used to play in the movies?
Yes.
And Duke made a record of this and the record now sells for fifty dollars.
No kidding.
And I could show you a copy except for the fact that I gave it to Jimmy Owens for his birthday and one of King Oliver too. And I knew that I could get more from Harrison Smith. So I thought this
might be a little interesting thing for Jimmy Smith, I mean, Smith, listen to that. (LAUGHTER). Jimmy Owens. And out of the ordinary.
